opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it really gets at why we developed neural operators in the first place.

When you think about physical phenomena like fluid flow, weather, or materials deformation, the dependencies are fundamentally multi-scale. You have very local interactions, like turbulence in a small eddy, but you also have long-range, global interactions, like pressure waves propagating across a whole domain or atmospheric patterns that span continents. A standard convolutional network captures local structure well, but it struggles with those global dependencies unless you stack many layers, and even then it's tied to a fixed grid resolution.

What we did with the Fourier Neural Operator was to say: let's work in the frequency domain. A convolution in physical space becomes a multiplication in Fourier space, so with a single layer you can capture global interactions across the entire domain. We combine that with local pointwise operations, so you get both the global, low-frequency structure and the local, fine-grained detail. And crucially, because we're learning an operator, a mapping between function spaces, rather than a mapping between fixed-size vectors, the model is discretization-invariant. You can train at one resolution and evaluate at a higher one, which is essential when the underlying physics is continuous.

On the temporal side, there are a couple of ways to approach it. One is to treat time as another dimension and learn the full space-time operator directly. The other is autoregressive: learn the operator that maps the state at one time to the state at the next, then roll it out. The autoregressive approach is flexible, but errors can accumulate over long horizons, so a lot of our work has gone into stability: making sure the learned dynamics respect things like conservation laws and don't drift or blow up. That's partly why we incorporate physics-informed losses: if you know the governing PDE, you can penalize violations at any resolution, even beyond the training data.

So the way I think about it is: physics is continuous, multi-scale, and governed by both local and global interactions across space and time. Neural operators are designed to respect all of that by construction, rather than hoping a generic architecture figures it out from data alone. That's what lets us get these huge speedups, sometimes orders of magnitude over traditional numerical solvers, while still being faithful to the underlying physics.

r001.rationale: It describes pressure waves propagating across the whole domain, communicating that an effect can spread from one location to others.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the right way to think about it is that, when you're dealing with physical systems like fluid flow or weather, the dependencies are fundamentally multi-scale and nonlocal. A standard convolutional network has a fixed, local receptive field. You stack layers to grow it, but you're still implicitly tied to a particular grid resolution. Neural operators take a different view: we're learning a mapping between function spaces, so the model should be defined independently of how you happen to discretize the input.

Spatially, that's why we went to the Fourier domain in the Fourier Neural Operator. In Fourier space, a convolution becomes a pointwise multiplication, so every layer is global. A low-frequency mode in the atmosphere can interact with something on the other side of the globe in a single layer. And because you parameterize the kernel in terms of frequency modes rather than grid points, you can train at one resolution and evaluate at another. The learned operator doesn't care whether you give it a 64 by 64 grid or a 256 by 256 grid. That's what we mean by discretization invariance.

Temporally, there are really two ways to go. One is to treat time as another dimension and learn the full space-time operator at once, which works well when you have the whole trajectory and want to capture long-range temporal correlations directly. The other is autoregressive, where you learn the evolution operator that maps the state at one time to the state at the next, and you roll it out. That's what we did for weather with FourCastNet. The challenge there is error accumulation, because small mistakes compound over many steps. So you think carefully about the time step you choose, you train with multi-step rollouts, and you make sure the model respects the physics well enough that the errors don't blow up.

The deeper principle is that physics tells us these dependencies have structure. There are conservation laws, there's symmetry, there are characteristic scales. The more of that we can bake into the architecture, rather than forcing the network to rediscover it from data, the better it generalizes. That's really the goal: a model that learns the solution operator of the underlying PDE, not just a pattern matcher on one dataset.

r001.rationale: The response says convolutional layers can grow a local receptive field and that Fourier layers are global, allowing interactions across the globe in a single layer.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that space and time are coupled. If you think about a fluid, what happens at one location depends on the surrounding flow, but it can also depend on what’s happening much farther away. And those interactions evolve over time, often at very different scales. You might have small, fast fluctuations alongside large structures that evolve slowly.

With neural operators, we want to learn a mapping between functions—for example, from the current velocity field to a future velocity field—rather than just a mapping between fixed-size vectors. That gives us a way to represent spatial interactions without tying the model to one particular grid. In a Fourier neural operator, the Fourier representation lets us capture global spatial interactions, and we combine that with local operations.

But capturing spatial structure well doesn’t automatically mean you get the temporal dynamics right. When you repeatedly use a model’s prediction as its next input, errors can accumulate. So we need to think about stability, the range of timescales in the system, and whether the model preserves the relevant physics over long trajectories. A good next-step prediction is useful, but ultimately we want the evolution to remain physically meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response describes spatial interactions reaching faraway locations and evolving over time, but does not state that an initially local effect eventually influences other locations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as two closely related questions: how do different parts of a system influence one another, and how does that influence evolve over time? In a fluid, for example, what happens at one location can affect what happens elsewhere, across many different spatial scales. So you need to capture both local interactions and longer-range dependencies.

With neural operators, we’re learning a mapping between functions. The input might be an initial condition, and the output might be the state of the system at a later time. The operator needs to capture the spatial structure of those fields as well as the dynamics connecting them. You can learn a time-stepping operator and apply it repeatedly, or learn a mapping over a whole space-time domain.

The challenge is that a model can look accurate over one time step and still accumulate errors when you roll it forward. So capturing temporal dependencies also means getting the underlying dynamics right—how information propagates, how different scales interact, and whether the prediction stays stable over longer horizons.

r001.rationale: It says an event at one location can affect elsewhere, but does not clearly state that an initially local effect spreads to other locations over time.
